paragraphs: “I was going to Father’s, but I meant to go to Katerina Ivanovna’s first.”

“To her, and to Father! Oh! What a coincidence! Why was I waiting for you? Why was I hungering and thirsting for you in every corner of my soul, even in my ribs? To send you to Father and to her, Katerina Ivanovna, so I could be done with her and with Father. To send an angel. I could have sent anyone, but I wanted to send an angel. And here you are, on your way to see Father and her.”
“Did you really mean to send me?” cried Alyosha, looking distressed.
“Wait! You knew it! And I can see you understand it all at once. But be quiet, be quiet for a while. Don’t be sorry, and don’t cry.”
Dmitri stood up, thought for a moment, and put his finger to his forehead.
“She’s asked you, she’s written you a letter or something, and that’s why you’re going to her? You wouldn’t be going except for that?”
“Here is her note.” Alyosha took it out of his pocket. Mitya read it quickly.

“And you were going the back way! Oh, gods, I thank you for sending him by the back way, and he came to me like the golden fish to the silly old fisherman in the fable! Listen, Alyosha, listen, brother! Now I mean to tell you everything, because I have to tell someone. I’ve already told an angel in heaven, but I want to tell an angel on earth. You are an angel on earth. You’ll hear me, and judge me, and forgive me. And that’s what I need, for someone above me to forgive me. Listen! Suppose two people break away from everything on earth and fly off into the unknown, or at least one of them does. And before flying off, or going to ruin, he goes to someone else and says, ‘Do this for me’—some favor never asked before, one that could only be asked on a deathbed. Would the other refuse, if he were a friend or a brother?”
“I’ll do it, but tell me what it is, and be quick,” said Alyosha.

“Be quick! Hm!... Don’t be in a hurry, Alyosha, you hurry and worry yourself. There’s no need to hurry now. Now the world has taken a new turn. Ah, Alyosha, what a pity you can’t understand ecstasy. But what am I saying to him? As if you didn’t understand it. What an ass I am! What am I saying? ‘Be noble, O man!’—who says that?”
Alyosha made up his mind to wait. He felt that perhaps his work really did lie here. Mitya sank into thought for a moment, with his elbow on the table and his head in his hand. Both were silent.

“Alyosha,” said Mitya, “you’re the only one who won’t laugh. I’d like to begin—my confession—with Schiller’s _Hymn to Joy_, _An die Freude_! I don’t know German, I only know it’s called that. Don’t think I’m talking nonsense because I’m drunk. I’m not a bit drunk. Brandy’s all very well, but I need two bottles to get drunk:
Silenus with his rosy face Upon his stumbling ass.

But I haven’t drunk even a quarter of a bottle, and I’m not Silenus. I’m not Silenus, though I am strong,[1] because I’ve made a decision once and for all. Forgive the pun; you’ll have to forgive me a lot more than puns today. Don’t worry. I’m not dragging it out. I’m talking sense, and I’ll come to the point in a minute. I won’t keep you in suspense. Wait, how does it go?”
He raised his head, thought for a minute, and began with enthusiasm:

“Wild and fearful in his cavern Hid the naked cave-man, And the homeless nomad wandered Laying waste the fertile plain. Menacing with spear and arrow The hunter roamed the woods.... Woe to all poor wretches stranded On those cruel and hostile shores!

“From the peak of high Olympus Mother Ceres came down, Seeking in those savage lands Her lost daughter Proserpine. But the Goddess found no refuge, Found no kindly welcome there, And no temple bearing witness To the worship of the gods.

“From the fields and from the vineyards Came no fruits to deck the feasts, Only the flesh of bloodstained victims Smoldered on the altar-fires, And wherever the grieving goddess Turns her melancholy gaze, Sunk in the vilest degradation Man displays his loathsomeness.”
Mitya broke into sobs and seized Alyosha’s hand.

“My dear, my dear, in degradation, in degradation now, too. There’s a terrible amount of suffering for man on earth, a terrible lot of trouble. Don’t think I’m only a brute in an officer’s uniform, wallowing in dirt and drink. I hardly think of anything but that degraded man—if only I’m not lying. I pray God I’m not lying and showing off. I think about that man because I am that man myself.
If he would purge his soul of vileness And attain to light and worth, He must turn and cling forever To his ancient Mother Earth.

But the difficulty is, how am I to cling forever to Mother Earth? I don’t kiss her. I don’t cling to her breast. Am I to become a peasant or a shepherd? I go on and I don’t know whether I’m going to shame or to light and joy. That’s the trouble, because everything in the world is a riddle! And whenever I’ve happened to sink into the vilest degradation (and it’s always happening), I always read that poem about Ceres and man. Has it reformed me? Never! Because I’m a Karamazov. When I leap into the pit, I go headlong with my heels up, and I’m pleased to be falling in that degrading position, and I take pride in it. And in the very depths of that degradation I begin a hymn of praise. Let me be cursed. Let me be vile and base, only let me kiss the hem of the veil in which my God is wrapped. Though I may be following the devil, I am Your son, O Lord, and I love You, and I feel the joy without which the world cannot stand.

Joy everlasting nourishes The soul of all creation, Her secret ferment fires The cup of life with flame. At her beck the grass has turned Each blade toward the light And solar systems have evolved From chaos and dark night, Filling the realms of boundless space Beyond the sage’s sight. At bountiful Nature’s kindly breast, All things that breathe drink Joy, And birds and beasts and creeping things All follow where she leads. Her gifts to man are friends in need, The wreath, the foaming must, To angels—a vision of God’s throne, To insects—sensual lust.

But enough poetry! I’m in tears; let me cry. It may be foolishness that everyone would laugh at. But you won’t laugh. Your eyes are shining, too. Enough poetry. I want to tell you now about the insects to whom God gave “sensual lust.”
To insects—sensual lust.

I am that insect, brother, and it was said of me especially. All we Karamazovs are such insects, and, angel as you are, that insect lives in you, too, and will stir up a storm in your blood. Storms, because sensual lust is a storm—worse than a storm! Beauty is a terrible and awful thing! It is terrible because it can’t be fathomed and never can be, for God sets us nothing but riddles. Here the boundaries meet and all contradictions lie side by side. I’m not a cultivated man, brother, but I’ve thought a lot about this. It’s terrible, the mysteries there are! Too many riddles weigh men down on earth. We must solve them as best we can, and try to come out of the water dry. Beauty! I can’t stand the thought that a man of lofty mind and heart begins with the ideal of the Madonna and ends with the ideal of Sodom. What’s still more awful is that a man with the ideal of Sodom in his soul does not give up the ideal of the Madonna, and his heart may burn with that ideal, truly burn, just as in his days of youth and innocence. Yes, man is broad, too broad, in fact. I’d make him narrower. The devil only knows what to make of it! What the mind finds shameful, the heart finds to be beauty and nothing else. Is there beauty in Sodom? Believe me, for the vast mass of mankind, beauty is found in Sodom. Did you know that secret? The awful thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there, and the battlefield is the heart of man. But a man always talks about his own ache. Listen, now, let’s come to the facts.”
